key_points.point: The authors propose a formal mechanism design framework to enforce AI safety requirements, treating regulation as a game between a regulator and a model provider. By using 'testing-by-betting' and credal sets, they aim to force providers to prove their model's safety by betting capital on it. This framework is designed to ensure that only compliant models gain market access, effectively creating a rigorous, mathematically grounded governance system.
key_points.verbatim: In this work, we formalise this problem by casting AI regulation as a mechanism design problem under uncertainty. We propose regulation mechanisms which push the burden of proof on the providers. key_points.point: The document asserts that information asymmetry is a fundamental challenge in AI regulation, as providers know significantly more about their models' pitfalls than regulators do. This asymmetry allows providers to act strategically to bypass safety standards. The authors argue that without a formal mechanism to account for this, regulators will be unable to prevent the deployment of unsafe models.
key_points.verbatim: At the same time, model providers possess much more knowledge than regulators about model's abilities and pitfalls. This creates an information asymmetry between providers and regulators which can be exploited by the model providers (Casper et al., 2024; Li & Goel, 2025).

key_points.point: The authors define 'perfect market outcomes' as a state where non-compliant providers are forced to self-exclude while compliant ones are encouraged to participate. They prove that this is only possible if the set of non-compliant distributions forms a 'credal set' (a closed, convex set of probability measures). This provides a mathematical threshold for when a regulatory requirement is actually enforceable.

This result connects mechanism design and imprecise probability by establishing a duality between regulation mechanisms and the set of non-compliant distributions.
